name: first-hour
alt: Cordon tape across a wet office corridor with a hazard sign and the lights left off, before any equipment has arrived
prompt:
A real documentary photograph taken inside a commercial office in the first hour after water was discovered, before any restoration crew has arrived. Portrait orientation, shot down a corridor or an open floor so the space runs away from the camera.

Dark saturated low-pile carpet tiles with shallow standing water spreading from a service riser cupboard whose door is open, exposing pipework. Red and white hazard barrier tape strung across the corridor at waist height between a column and a filing cabinet, with a folding yellow wet-floor sign set behind it. The overhead lights in the affected bay are OFF while the bay beyond is still lit, so the taped-off area reads darker than the space behind it. A few cardboard document boxes have been lifted onto a desktop clear of the floor, and two office chairs are pushed well back from the wet area.

NO restoration equipment anywhere in frame: no air movers, no dehumidifiers, no ducting, no extraction hose. NO technicians, no crew, no hands. This is the problem before anyone started work. One office worker may appear small and far away in the lit bay beyond the tape, turned away from camera, but nobody is near the water.

Lighting is ordinary office fluorescent troffers in the far bay, flat and slightly green, plus grey daylight from a window. The taped-off foreground is dim and under-lit. No sunbeams, no golden hour, no lens flare, no bright highlights.

Deliberately unglamorous: scuffed skirting trunking, a dented filing cabinet, a coiled extension lead, water creeping up the base of a plasterboard partition, a stained ceiling tile overhead where the water came through. Surfaces look used — not new, not polished, not reflective.

Shot on a 28mm lens at f/4, handheld and slightly off-level, mild sensor noise, natural white balance left uncorrected. Plain realistic colour, no grading. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no readable signage beyond a generic wet-floor symbol.

3:4 portrait, roughly 1200 × 1600. Water has faint dull broken reflections, never a glossy mirror sheen. If it looks like a staged stock photo it is wrong — it should look like a facilities manager documented it on arrival.
